teachingRecords.name: Adeels Palace v Moubarak
teachingRecords.facts: After a fight in a nightclub on New Year's Eve, Moubarak was shot by another patron. He argued that the club was negligent in not providing any security, resulting in his injury.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether the club's failure to provide security was a cause of the shooting injuries under CLA s 5D(1), and if not, whether it was an exceptional case under s 5D(2).
teachingRecords.held: The 'but for' test was not satisfied: the evidence at trial did not show that the presence of security personnel would have deterred or prevented the re-entry of the gunman. There was no reason to treat the case as an exceptional case under s 5D(2).
teachingRecords.ratio: In contrast to what Mason CJ observed in March v Stramare, s 5D(1) 'treats factual causation and scope of liability as separate and distinct issues', and factual causation under s 5D(1) is determined by the 'but for' test. That changing 'any of the circumstances in which the shootings occurred might have made a difference does not prove factual causation'; it 'would be contrary to established principles' to hold the defendant responsible when negligence was not a necessary condition but 'might have' prevented the harm [57].
teachingRecords.significance: The leading High Court statement that s 5D(1) separates factual causation from scope of liability, and the one case on the slides in which s 5D(2) was considered and found not to apply.
teachingRecords.why-here: Cite for the 'but for' test under s 5D(1)(a), for keeping factual causation separate from scope of liability, and for "might have made a difference" not being enough — including under s 5D(2).

cases.plain: The club could only be made to pay for these injuries if the missing security probably made a causal difference. Saying guards might have stopped the gunman leaves that question unanswered.

cases.name: Amaca Pty Ltd v Booth
cases.citation: Amaca Pty Ltd v Booth (2011) 246 CLR 36

teachingRecords.name: Amaca v Booth
teachingRecords.facts: Booth had mesothelioma and 30 years of exposure to asbestos in brake linings manufactured by Amaca (about 27 years of heavy brake-lining exposure; his other exposures were trivial by comparison). The Dust Diseases Tribunal drew an "overwhelming inference" of causation.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether an inference that Amaca's asbestos caused or contributed to Booth's mesothelioma was open when science could not say which exposure triggered the disease.
teachingRecords.held: The Court of Appeal and the High Court upheld the Tribunal's inference. French CJ held that Booth's exposure to asbestos in brake linings manufactured by Amaca not only prospectively increased the risk of his contracting the disease but, in the event, [causally] contributed to its development and continuation.
teachingRecords.ratio: A causal connection may be inferred from medical and expert evidence (French CJ also referred to the 'Bradford Hill criteria' as circumstantial evidence of a causal relationship between asbestos and mesothelioma). The inference was reasonably open because asbestos is effectively the only known cause of mesothelioma, Booth's heavy exposure dwarfed his other exposures, and expert evidence accepted at trial was that cumulative exposure contributes to the disease.
teachingRecords.significance: Material contribution established in a dust disease case; contrasted with Amaca v Ellis. The CLA is never mentioned because s 3B(1) excludes dust disease proceedings under the Dust Diseases Tribunal Act 1989 (NSW).
teachingRecords.why-here: Cite where the evidence supports an inference that the defendant's exposure contributed to the disease, not merely increased the risk.

cases.plain: The experts supported a conclusion that the asbestos Booth actually breathed helped cause his disease. The court did not need to identify one decisive fibre.

cases.name: Amaca Pty Ltd v Ellis
cases.citation: Amaca Pty Ltd v Ellis (2010) 240 CLR 111

teachingRecords.name: Amaca Pty Ltd v Ellis
teachingRecords.aglc: Amaca Pty Ltd v Ellis (2010) 240 CLR 111
teachingRecords.facts: The claimant developed lung cancer. He had been exposed to asbestos and had also smoked. The evidence was limited exposure, mainly epidemiological (risk) evidence, and a competing cause (smoking).
teachingRecords.issue: Whether showing that the asbestos exposure increased the risk of lung cancer was enough to establish causation.
teachingRecords.held: Showing that exposure increased the risk is not sufficient. The claimant must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the exposure actually contributed to the cancer, and the evidence in the case could not establish this.
teachingRecords.ratio: Risk alone is not enough: an increase in the risk of harm does not establish factual causation without proof, on the balance of probabilities, that the defendant's conduct contributed to the harm.
teachingRecords.significance: The High Court's rejection of a risk-based test of causation; contrasted on the slides with Amaca v Booth. The textbook flowchart lists it under material contribution to harm.
teachingRecords.why-here: Cite where the evidence shows only an increased risk — especially with a competing cause — to argue causation fails.

cases.oneLine: Asbestos-related statistical risk did not prove that asbestos caused this smoker’s lung cancer.
cases.plain: Asbestos can increase the chance of lung cancer without the evidence proving it helped cause this particular cancer. Smoking was a competing explanation, and the claimant still bore the burden of proof.
cases.concreteExplanation: Think of a risk study as describing a group. The legal question asks what probably happened to this individual; a group association needs evidence connecting the exposure to that individual’s disease.
keyFacts: The claimant developed lung cancer. He had been exposed to asbestos and had also smoked. The evidence was limited exposure, mainly epidemiological (risk) evidence, and a competing cause (smoking).

reasoning: Risk alone is not enough: an increase in the risk of harm does not establish factual causation without proof, on the balance of probabilities, that the defendant's conduct contributed to the harm.

cases.outcome: Showing that exposure increased the risk is not sufficient. The claimant must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the exposure actually contributed to the cancer, and the evidence in the case could not establish this.
cases.ratio: Risk alone is not enough: an increase in the risk of harm does not establish factual causation without proof, on the balance of probabilities, that the defendant's conduct contributed to the harm.
limits: The case does not make epidemiology legally irrelevant; it rejects the inference on the evidence presented.
Distinguish the different disease and cumulative-exposure evidence in Booth.

teachingRecords.name: Benic v NSW
teachingRecords.facts: Not given in the materials: the Topic 9 slides use the case only for Garling J's framework. The slides say it is in the casebook, but the casebook supplied covers topics 1–6 only.
teachingRecords.issue: How the breach question is to be determined under s 5B of the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW).
teachingRecords.held: Not stated in the materials; the lecture uses the case for its guidance on method, not its outcome.
teachingRecords.ratio: Garling J: "The three separate elements in s 5B(1) represent the concepts of foreseeability, probability and reasonableness of precautions … These concepts are each represented in the common law, and are often conflated in the term 'reasonable foreseeability' but the statute now makes it clear that each must be separately addressed." Step 1 is to identify a risk of harm — it is sufficient "if the risk of harm is described as a class of injury, as distinct from the particular injury actually suffered by the plaintiff"; step 2 is to consider the three elements in s 5B.
teachingRecords.significance: The framework for a breach answer under the Act: identify the risk, then address (a), (b) and (c) separately.
teachingRecords.why-here: Cite it to open a breach answer: name the risk of harm as a class of injury before applying s 5B(1).

cases.oneLine: Identify the risk, then address all three statutory breach thresholds separately.
cases.plain: Benic blamed the absence of early psychological treatment after death threats. The court rejected his claim: he had not established negligence or that earlier intervention probably would have prevented the PTSD.
cases.concreteExplanation: Keep two questions separate: what reasonable precautions were required, and whether those precautions probably would have changed the outcome. Benic’s structured breach method cannot replace proof of causation.
keyFacts: Benic was a NSW police officer providing close protection to the Premier. He received serious death threats and developed PTSD.
He alleged that prompt referral for psychiatric or psychological treatment would have prevented his condition and work incapacity.
cases.issue: How should s 5B be applied, and did the alleged failure to arrange early psychiatric intervention cause Benic’s PTSD?
reasoning: Garling J: "The three separate elements in s 5B(1) represent the concepts of foreseeability, probability and reasonableness of precautions … These concepts are each represented in the common law, and are often conflated in the term 'reasonable foreseeability' but the statute now makes it clear that each must be separately addressed." Step 1 is to identify a risk of harm — it is sufficient "if the risk of harm is described as a class of injury, as distinct from the particular injury actually suffered by the plaintiff"; step 2 is to consider the three elements in s 5B.
At [623], the evidence did not establish on the balance of probabilities that early intervention would have succeeded. Possibility of benefit was insufficient.
cases.outcome: Judgment for the defendant. Benic failed to prove the Commissioner’s negligence and failed to prove that, but for the alleged omission, he would not have suffered PTSD. The damages discussion was not an award to him.
cases.ratio: Garling J: "The three separate elements in s 5B(1) represent the concepts of foreseeability, probability and reasonableness of precautions … These concepts are each represented in the common law, and are often conflated in the term 'reasonable foreseeability' but the statute now makes it clear that each must be separately addressed." The Commissioner’s protective duty and the State’s vicarious liability were distinguished; the State was not described as Benic’s direct employer.

teachingRecords.held: It was enough that the negligent exposure made a contribution that was more than de minimis (or negligible). The claimant need not show it was the sole or main cause.

teachingRecords.name: Bryan v Maloney
teachingRecords.facts: A builder constructed a house with defective foundations. Mrs Maloney, who was the third owner since the construction, noticed cracks in the walls due to the defective foundations.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether a builder owes a subsequent purchaser of a house a duty of care to avoid pure economic loss.
teachingRecords.held: The High Court ruled that a builder owed a duty of care to a subsequent purchaser to take reasonable care in the building of a house.
teachingRecords.ratio: Using the proximity principle, a builder of a dwelling owes a subsequent purchaser a duty to take reasonable care in its construction, to avoid pure economic loss from latent defects.
teachingRecords.significance: Drew a distinction between the construction of dwellings and other buildings (a homeowner being more vulnerable and less sophisticated); reconsidered in Woolcock.
teachingRecords.why-here: The common law authority for a duty to a later homeowner for latent defects.

cases.concreteExplanation: Follow the house rather than the contracts: builder → first owner → later owners → Maloney. The foundations remain hidden throughout, so the absence of a direct building contract did not end the duty inquiry.

cases.citation: Caltex Refineries (Qld) Pty Ltd v Stavar (2009) 75 NSWLR 649

teachingRecords.name: Caltex Refineries (Qld) Pty Ltd v Stavar
teachingRecords.aglc: Caltex Refineries (Qld) Pty Ltd v Stavar (2009) 75 NSWLR 649
teachingRecords.facts:
Mrs Stavar's husband was exposed to asbestos while working at an oil refinery. When Mrs Stavar washed his
contaminated work clothes at home, she was exposed to asbestos dust and later developed cancer. Because
Mrs Stavar was not the refinery's employee, but the employee's wife, the case fell outside the established
employer/employee category of duty.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether an employer owes a duty of care to a person outside the established employer/employee relationship — here, an employee's spouse exposed to asbestos through home laundering of contaminated work clothes.
teachingRecords.held:
The NSW Court of Appeal held that a duty of care could be found on the facts, applying the "salient
features" approach because the case was novel. The Court set out a non-exhaustive list of salient factors
relevant to whether a duty should be recognised, including foreseeability, control, vulnerability, reliance,
assumption of responsibility, proximity, the category of relationship, the nature and danger of the
defendant's activity, the defendant's knowledge, indeterminacy of liability, and coherence with statute and
the common law.
teachingRecords.ratio: Where a case is novel — falling outside an established category of relationship — Australian courts determine whether a duty of care exists by weighing a non-exhaustive list of "salient features" of the relationship between the parties, rather than by reasonable foreseeability alone.
teachingRecords.significance: Leading NSW Court of Appeal authority setting out the salient features approach used in every novel duty of care case in Australia.
teachingRecords.why-here: The authority that supplies the actual list of salient factors to work through whenever a duty of care problem falls outside an established category.

teachingRecords.name: Chapman v Hearse
teachingRecords.facts:
A car driven by Chapman collided with another vehicle near an Adelaide intersection; Chapman's vehicle
overturned and he was thrown onto the roadway, unconscious. Dr Cherry, driving a third car that stopped, went
to aid the unconscious Chapman on a dark, wet night with poor visibility and no one to warn oncoming traffic.
While attending to Chapman, Dr Cherry was struck by a car driven by Hearse and died of his injuries. Dr
Cherry's executor sued Hearse, who joined Chapman as a third party claiming contribution.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether Chapman owed Dr Cherry a duty of care, given that Chapman could not have foreseen the precise sequence of events that led to Dr Cherry's death.
teachingRecords.held:
The High Court (Dixon CJ, Kitto, Taylor, Menzies and Windeyer JJ) dismissed Chapman's appeal against the
order for contribution, rejecting his argument that he owed no duty of care to Dr Cherry. The test for the
existence of a duty of care does not require reasonable foreseeability of the precise sequence of events or
the precise manner in which the injury was sustained; it was enough that injury to a class of persons of
which Dr Cherry was one — a person likely to render aid at the scene of a road accident — might reasonably
have been foreseen as a consequence of the collision.
teachingRecords.ratio: To establish a duty of care, it is not necessary to show that the precise manner in which the plaintiff's injuries were sustained was reasonably foreseeable; it is sufficient that injury to a class of persons of which the plaintiff was one might reasonably have been foreseen as a consequence of the defendant's conduct.
teachingRecords.significance: Leading Australian authority on what "reasonable foreseeability" requires at the duty stage — foreseeability of a general class of harm and class of person, not of the exact chain of events.
teachingRecords.why-here: The go-to authority whenever a defendant argues they could not have foreseen the exact way an injury occurred.

teachingRecords.aglc: Crimmins v Stevedoring Industry Finance Committee (1999) 200 CLR 1
teachingRecords.facts: Crimmins worked as a waterside worker at Port Melbourne 1961–65. Stevedoring operations were regulated by the Australian Stevedoring Industry Authority, which directed workers where to work. The Authority was later abolished and the Stevedoring Industry Finance Committee (SIFC) assumed its liabilities. In 1997 Crimmins was diagnosed with mesothelioma caused by unloading asbestos cargoes. The Authority was not his employer.
teachingRecords.issue: Did the Authority owe Crimmins a duty of care, and did its liability pass to the SIFC?
teachingRecords.held: The High Court held that a duty of care was owed, because the Authority/SIFC had an overarching supervisory and regulatory role regarding safety, and individual employers were required to supply safety equipment. (The lecture adds that the liability did pass to the SIFC, which stands in the Authority's shoes.) Hayne J dissented: no duty was owed in deciding whether to exercise the quasi-legislative power to order the use of respirators.
teachingRecords.ratio: McHugh J: the statutory authority owed a duty because it directed the worker to places of work with risks of injury of which it was, or ought to have been, aware, and it knew or ought to have known he was specially vulnerable — through the casual nature of his employment and his obligation to obey its directions.
teachingRecords.significance: Source of McHugh J's six questions for whether a statutory authority owes an affirmative duty in a novel case (foreseeability, power to protect a specific class, vulnerability, knowledge, core policy functions, other policy reasons).

cases.name: Donoghue v Stevenson
cases.citation: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562

teachingRecords.name: Donoghue v Stevenson
teachingRecords.facts:
In August 1928, Mrs Donoghue went with a friend to a café in Scotland for an ice-cream soda; the friend
bought her the ice cream and a bottle of ginger beer. The ginger beer came in an opaque glass bottle bearing
the manufacturer's name, David Stevenson. As the beer was poured into a tumbler, a decomposed snail floated
out of the bottle. Donoghue suffered shock and severe gastro-enteritis and sued the manufacturer, with whom
she had no contract (her friend had paid).
teachingRecords.issue: Whether a manufacturer of a product, with whom the ultimate consumer has no contract, can owe that consumer a duty of care in negligence.
teachingRecords.held:
The House of Lords, by a 3:2 majority, allowed Donoghue's appeal. A manufacturer who sells products intending
them to reach the ultimate consumer in the form in which they left the manufacturer, with no reasonable
possibility of intermediate examination, and knowing that a lack of reasonable care in preparing the product
will injure the consumer, owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.
teachingRecords.ratio:
Lord Atkin's neighbour principle: a person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which they
can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure their "neighbour" — a person so closely and directly
affected by the act that the defendant ought reasonably to have them in contemplation when directing their
mind to the act or omission in question.
teachingRecords.significance: Founding authority of the modern tort of negligence; established that a manufacturer owes consumers a duty of care independent of any contract between them.
teachingRecords.why-here: The starting point for every duty of care question this unit tests — the neighbour principle that every problem answer opens with before moving to categories or salient factors.

cases.plain: Donoghue alleged that an unseen snail in bottled ginger beer made her ill. Her friend paid, but the lack of a purchase contract with the manufacturer did not prevent a negligence duty.
cases.concreteExplanation: Track access to the defect: the opaque bottle prevented reasonable intermediate inspection before consumption. The decision allowed the legal claim to proceed on assumed allegations; it did not prove that the snail existed.

The bottle was opaque. Donoghue alleged that a decomposed snail emerged and that she suffered shock and gastroenteritis.
The appeal addressed whether those assumed allegations disclosed a legal claim, not whether the alleged snail and resulting illness were proved.

teachingRecords.name: Grant v Australian Knitting Mills
teachingRecords.aglc: Grant v Australian Knitting Mills [1936] AC 85
teachingRecords.facts:
Dr Grant bought woollen underpants from a retailer who had purchased them from the manufacturer, Australian
Knitting Mills. He wore them for a day and began to itch; within a week he developed dermatitis so severe
that he spent seventeen weeks in hospital. The garments contained free sulphites, a chemical irritant left
in through negligence in manufacturing, which was a hidden and latent defect not detectable by any
reasonable examination. Grant won at trial, but the High Court held the evidence insufficient; he appealed
to the Privy Council.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether the manufacturer of a product with a hidden defect owed the ultimate consumer a duty of care, applying Donoghue v Stevenson, and whether that principle extends beyond food or drink to garments worn externally.
teachingRecords.held:
The appeal was allowed. Applying Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council held the manufacturer owed Dr Grant
a duty of care: the case fell squarely within Lord Atkin's principle, the sulphites being a hidden defect
like the snail in the opaque bottle. It was immaterial that the garment was worn externally rather than
consumed internally, or that Dr Grant also had a contract claim against the retailer; the manufacturer's
duty arises independently of contract, provided the product reaches the consumer with no reasonable
possibility of intermediate examination.
teachingRecords.ratio: A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer of its product wherever a hidden, undetectable defect caused by negligent manufacture reaches the consumer without any reasonable possibility of intermediate examination, regardless of whether the product is consumed internally or applied externally.

teachingRecords.why-here: The standard second authority (after Donoghue) for the established manufacturer/consumer category of duty of care.

teachingRecords.name: Hargrave v Goldman
teachingRecords.facts:
Lightning struck a red gum tree on the defendant's Western Australian farm. The defendant had the tree
felled but left the resulting fire to burn itself out. The weather then turned, the fire revived, and it
spread to destroy the plaintiff's neighbouring properties.
teachingRecords.issue:
Whether an occupier who did not create a natural danger, but knew of it and did not act, owed neighbouring
occupiers a duty of care for harm caused by the omission to abate it.
teachingRecords.held:
The lecture material identifies the relevant factors for liability — reasonable foreseeability of harm,
the occupier-neighbour special relationship, the defendant's knowledge of the danger, and their control
over it — as the ingredients needed for an omission-based duty of care in this setting.
teachingRecords.ratio:
An omission to abate a danger on one's land can found a duty of care to neighbouring occupiers where there
is a special relationship (here, occupier-neighbour), the defendant knew of the danger, and had the
practical ability (control) to deal with it — foreseeability alone is not enough.
teachingRecords.significance:
Establishes the extra ingredients — special relationship, knowledge and control — that must be added to
foreseeability before an omission attracts a duty of care.
teachingRecords.why-here: Used to show what must be added to foreseeability before an omission (rather than a positive act) attracts a duty of care.

cases.oneLine: Knowledge and control of a natural danger on land can support a duty to neighbouring occupiers.
cases.plain: Goldman did not cause the lightning strike, but he knew the tree was burning and controlled the land. The issue was what reasonable action he should take once the danger existed.
cases.concreteExplanation: Separate creation from response: lightning creates fire → occupier learns of fire → occupier has an opportunity to act → fire spreads. An omission at the response stage can matter even though nature created the first danger.
keyFacts:
Lightning struck a red gum tree on the defendant's Western Australian farm. The defendant had the tree
felled but left the resulting fire to burn itself out. The weather then turned, the fire revived, and it
spread to destroy the plaintiff's neighbouring properties.

The occupier initially arranged felling, cleared combustible material and sprayed the area. The critical finding was that he could reasonably have extinguished the remaining fire by Monday morning but did not.
cases.issue:
Whether an occupier who did not create a natural danger, but knew of it and did not act, owed neighbouring
occupiers a duty of care for harm caused by the omission to abate it.
reasoning:
An omission to abate a danger on one's land can found a duty of care to neighbouring occupiers where there
is a special relationship (here, occupier-neighbour), the defendant knew of the danger, and had the
practical ability (control) to deal with it — foreseeability alone is not enough.

A lightning origin did not eliminate a reasonable-care duty once the danger was known and could be controlled. The statutory extinguishment provision did not itself create the claimed private cause of action.
cases.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; the WA Supreme Court judgment was set aside and the case remitted. The trial judge could consider an application to reopen liability with fresh evidence; assessment of damages depended on the liability findings remaining unchanged.
cases.ratio:
An omission to abate a danger on one's land can found a duty of care to neighbouring occupiers where there
is a special relationship (here, occupier-neighbour), the defendant knew of the danger, and had the
practical ability (control) to deal with it — foreseeability alone is not enough.
limits: The remittal permitted consideration of newly tendered evidence; it was not an unconditional final damages award.
Reasonableness and practical capacity matter: the initial precautionary steps were not themselves criticised.
cases.examUse: Used to show what must be added to foreseeability before an omission (rather than a positive act) attracts a duty of care.
pitfalls: Do not say Goldman created the lightning fire.
Do not infer that he took no precautions at all, or that statutory breach automatically supplied a civil action.

teachingRecords.name: Hedley Byrne v Heller
teachingRecords.facts:
Hedley Byrne, an advertising agency, asked its bank, National Provincial, to check the credit status of
Easipower Ltd with Easipower's own bank, Heller & Partners. Heller gave a favourable credit reference, but
expressly "without responsibility". Relying on that reference, Hedley Byrne extended credit to Easipower and
suffered loss when Easipower went into liquidation. Hedley Byrne sued Heller for negligent misstatement.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether a duty of care can arise for negligent words causing pure economic loss (loss not derived from personal injury or property damage), and, if so, whether such a duty existed on these facts.
teachingRecords.held:
The House of Lords held that a duty of care can arise where careless advice or information causes pure
economic loss, provided there is a special relationship between the parties involving a voluntary assumption
of responsibility by the party giving the advice and reasonable reliance by the other party. On the facts,
however, Hedley Byrne's claim failed because Heller had expressly disclaimed responsibility for the
reference.
teachingRecords.ratio: A duty of care for negligent misstatement causing pure economic loss can arise where there is a special relationship between the parties — a voluntary assumption of responsibility by the adviser, reliance by the other party, and reasonableness of that reliance — but an effective disclaimer of responsibility negates the duty.
teachingRecords.significance: Founding authority for duty of care in negligent misstatement and pure economic loss, extending negligence beyond the Donoghue v Stevenson paradigm of physical injury or property damage.
teachingRecords.why-here: The authority for every negligent-advice or negligent-misstatement problem question; its four elements structure the whole analysis.

cases.name: Imbree v McNeilly
cases.citation: Imbree v McNeilly [2008] HCA 40

teachingRecords.name: Imbree v McNeilly
teachingRecords.facts: Not given in the materials: the Topic 9 slides cite the case only for the proposition recorded below.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether a learner driver owes a lower standard of care than a licensed driver.
teachingRecords.held: As stated in the slides: the standard of care for a learner driver is the same as for a licensed driver.
teachingRecords.ratio: The standard is objective and impersonal: it does not vary with the particular driver's experience. It would be unworkable to apply a different standard to different drivers based on their experience level.
teachingRecords.significance: Inexperience does not lower the reasonable person standard.
teachingRecords.why-here: Cite it when a defendant pleads inexperience — a learner driver, a first-timer, a new volunteer.

cases.oneLine: A learner driver owes the ordinary objective driving standard; inexperience does not lower it.
cases.plain: McNeilly’s inexperience did not lower the driving standard owed to the passenger supervising him. The supervisor’s own carelessness was considered separately when damages were reduced.
cases.concreteExplanation: Use two columns: the driver’s objective standard, and the supervisor’s own precautions. Imbree does not solve one column by changing the legal test in the other.
keyFacts: Imbree allowed sixteen-year-old McNeilly, who had neither a licence nor learner permit, to drive a four-wheel drive on a Northern Territory gravel road.
While Imbree supervised from the front seat, McNeilly steered around tyre debris, then turned sharply and accelerated; the vehicle rolled. Imbree suffered spinal injury and tetraplegia.
cases.issue: Whether a learner driver owes a lower standard of care than a licensed driver.
reasoning: The objective standard is that of a reasonable driver; neither licence status nor inexperience lowers it.
A supervising passenger’s knowledge or failures may affect contributory negligence without reducing the driver’s standard.
cases.outcome: Imbree’s appeal was allowed; the ordinary reasonable-driver standard applied and Cook v Cook should no longer be followed. The Court adopted the trial allocation of 30% contributory negligence, with consequential orders to be settled.
cases.ratio: The standard is objective and impersonal: it does not vary with the particular driver's experience. It would be unworkable to apply a different standard to different drivers based on their experience level.
limits: The driver’s standard and the passenger’s contributory negligence are separate.
The Court did not decide every possible question about a person so incompetent that taking control itself is negligent.
cases.examUse: Cite it when a defendant pleads inexperience — a learner driver, a first-timer, a new volunteer.
pitfalls: Do not call McNeilly a licensed learner: he had no learner permit.
Do not confuse the restored 30% contributory-negligence allocation with the driver’s objective standard.

teachingRecords.name: Jones v Bartlett
teachingRecords.facts: The plaintiff, son of the tenant, was injured when he walked through a glass door. The glass door complied with the Australian standards at the time the house was built but not when it was leased; the landlord did not know that it did not comply with the regulations.
teachingRecords.issue: Whether the landlord owed a duty of care, and what its nature and extent were.
teachingRecords.held: The High Court held that the landlord owed a duty of care, but it was not breached: the glass door was not held to be a dangerous defect.
teachingRecords.ratio: Gummow and Hayne JJ: the content of the landlord's duty to the tenant is "conterminous with a requirement that the premises be reasonably fit for … habitation as a domestic residence"; it requires a landlord not to let premises with defects which the landlord knows or ought to know make them unsafe for the use, and is discharged if the landlord takes reasonable steps to ascertain such defects and reasonable steps to remove them or make the premises safe. A narrower duty is owed to other entrants.
teachingRecords.significance: The leading statement of the content of a landlord's duty: duty usually owed, the argument is about reasonable steps.
teachingRecords.why-here: The authority for any landlord problem — both the existence and the content of the duty.

cases.oneLine: An employer remained responsible for ensuring a safe work system despite engaging a crane contractor.
